5:8.note: Paul keeps the feast of unleavened bread in figure: the Church's azymes are sincerity and truth, against Exodus' seven days without leaven.

evidence.source: For our Pasch, Christ, is immolated
evidence.target: Go take a lamb by your families, and sacrifice the Phase

5:7.note: 'Our Pasch, Christ, is immolated': Paul names Christ himself the lamb Moses commanded Israel to take and sacrifice.

evidence.source: all in Moyses were baptized in the cloud and in the sea
evidence.target: went through the midst of the dry sea: for the water was as it were a wall on their right hand and their left

10:2.note: Paul argues that the crossing itself was Israel's baptism — 'all in Moses were baptized in the cloud and in the sea' — the doctrinal pattern on which his warning to Corinth rests.

evidence.source: nor the liers with mankind
evidence.target: He that lieth with man as if he should company with woman, both have committed abomination

6:9.note: Paul's single compound name for the vice is struck from Leviticus' own phrase — the man who 'lieth with mankind'. The list at Corinth is Paul's; the wording is the law's.

evidence.source: But the things that the heathen do immolate, to devils they do immolate, and not to God
evidence.target: and they shall no more immolate their hosts to devils, with whom they have committed fornication

10:20.note: Paul's charge that idol-sacrifice is devil-sacrifice is Leviticus 17:7's own verdict on Israel's sacrifices to the field devils, carried over to the Gentiles' tables.

evidence.source: But now Christ is risen again from the dead, the first fruits of them that sleep
evidence.target: you shall bring sheaves of ears, the first fruits of your harvest to the Priest

15:20.note: Paul names the risen Christ with the sheaf's title — the firstfruits of the harvest, which the priest lifts up before the Lord on the morrow after the sabbath (23:11): the very day of the resurrection.

evidence.source: Know you not that they which work in the holy place, eat the things that are of the holy place: and they that serve the altar, participate with the altar?
evidence.target: he shall eat it in the Holy place of the court of the tabernacle

9:13.note: Paul's case for the preacher's living rests on the Levitical arrangement itself: those who minister eat the holy things in the holy place (so also 7:6 for the priests' flesh). The argument is institutional rather than verbal — graded theme.

evidence.source: Behold Israel according to the flesh: they that eat the hosts, are they not partakers of the altar?
evidence.target: the flesh whereof shall be eaten the same day

10:18.note: Paul's altar-communion argument presupposes the peace offering's rule: the flesh is eaten by the offerers on the same day — eating the sacrifice is sharing the altar. What is true at Israel's altar is then turned against table-fellowship with idols.

evidence.source: Neither let us fornicate, as certain of them did fornicate, and there fell in one day three and twenty thousand
evidence.target: and there were slain four and twenty thousand men

10:8.note: Paul counts those who fell in one day at Phogor; Numbers gives the plague's whole toll — three and twenty thousand in the day, four and twenty thousand in all. The seed keys Paul's verse to the sin's opening (25:1); the reckoning of the dead is this verse.

evidence.source: we curse men which are made after the similitude of God
evidence.target: Let us make Man to our image & likeness

3:9.note: James forbids cursing men on Genesis' ground: they are made after the similitude of God.

evidence.source: said also, Thou shalt not kill
evidence.target: Thou shalt not murder

2:11.note: James quotes the sixth commandment; the DR text of Exodus renders the word 'murder' where James has 'kill'.

evidence.source: For he that said, Thou shalt not commit adultery
evidence.target: Thou shalt not commit adultery

2:11.note: James quotes the seventh commandment in the Decalogue's own words, to bind the whole Law to one Speaker.

evidence.source: Behold the hire of the work-men that have reaped your fields, which is defrauded of you, cryeth
evidence.target: The work of thy hireling shall not abide with thee until morning

5:4.note: The hire kept back is Leviticus' exact case — the hireling's wage held past its day. James hears the withheld wage itself crying out. Malachias names the same offence from the same verse (entered separately); Tobias 4:15's wage rule is own-carried.

evidence.source: God made man right, and he hath entangled himself with infinite questions
evidence.target: God created man to his own image

7:30.note: The Preacher sums up the fall in one line: God made man right — created to his image — and man has entangled himself.

evidence.source: If thou hast vowed any thing to God, defer not to pay it: for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeaseth him. But whatsoever thou hast vowed, pay it
evidence.target: he shall not make his word frustrate, but all that he promised he shall fulfill

5:3.note: The Preacher's counsel is the law's edge turned proverb: defer not to pay what thou hast vowed — the same duty this verse lays on the man who binds himself by an oath.

evidence.source: put on the new man which according to God is created in justice, and holiness of the truth
evidence.target: to the image of God he created him

4:24.note: The new man is created according to God, as man was first created to God's image: a creation renewed.

evidence.source: Hath not one God created us?
evidence.target: male and female he created them

2:10.note: Malachias argues brotherhood from the one creation: one God created them all, male and female — one human family under one Father, which is why despising a brother violates the covenant.

evidence.source: Was not Esau brother to Jacob, saith our Lord, and I loved Jacob
evidence.target: one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger

1:2.note: Malachias' 'I loved Jacob' is God's later word upon the oracle spoken before the twins were born: the elder shall serve the younger.

evidence.source: in every place there is sacrificing, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation
evidence.target: in every place where the memory of my name shall be: I will come to thee, and will bless thee

1:11.note: Exodus' altar law blesses 'every place where the memory of my name shall be'; Malachias sees the day when 'in every place there is offered to my name a clean oblation' among the Gentiles.

evidence.source: Behold I send mine Angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face
evidence.target: Behold I will send mine Angel, which shall go before thee

3:1.note: 'Behold I send mine Angel' — Malachias opens with the words of the promise that closes the book of the covenant: the Angel who goes before Israel into the promised place.

evidence.source: and them that calumniate the hire of the hired man, the widows, and pupils, and oppress the stranger
evidence.target: Thou shalt not calumniate thy neighbour, nor oppress him by violence. The work of thy hireling shall not abide with thee until morning

3:5.note: The prophet's witness-list is built from Leviticus 19:13 itself: 'calumniate' and the hired man's hire are the verse's own two halves, fused in one phrase.

evidence.source: If you offer the blind to be immolated, is it not evil? & if you offer the lame and the feeble is it not evil?
evidence.target: If it have a blemish, you shall not offer it, neither shall it be acceptable

1:8.note: The prophet's charge — blind, lame and feeble victims on the altar — is measured by the blemish law (spelled out at 22:22: the blind, the broken, the maimed). What would shame a governor's table profanes God's.

evidence.source: My covenant was with him of life and peace: & I gave him fear: and he feared me
evidence.target: Therefore speak to him: Behold I give him the peace of my covenant

2:5.note: The covenant 'of life and peace' Malachias recalls for Levi is this grant to Levi's zealous son: the peace of God's covenant, given to Phinees in the act of zeal.

evidence.source: She is a tree of life to them that shall apprehend her
evidence.target: the tree of life also in the middle of Paradise

3:18.note: Wisdom is praised in Eden's own title: a tree of life to them that lay hold on her.

evidence.source: When he prepared the heavens, I was present
evidence.target: In the beginning GOD created heaven and earth

8:27.note: Wisdom speaks as present when the heavens were prepared: Genesis' creation contemplated from within, by her who was with the Maker before the earth was made.

evidence.source: A deceitful balance, is abomination before God: and an equal weight is his will
evidence.target: Let the balance be just, and the weights equal, the bushel just, and the sextary equal

11:1.note: The proverb distils the holiness code's market law into one line: 'an equal weight is his will' is Leviticus' just balance in Solomon's dress. Amos and Micheas return to the same law (set aside as alternates).

evidence.source: The impious flyeth, no man pursuing: but the just confident as a lion, shall be without terror
evidence.target: You shall fly, when no man pursueth you

28:1.note: The covenant curse — flying, with no man pursuing — becomes the proverb's portrait of a guilty conscience. The just man's lion-like fearlessness is its mirror image.

evidence.source: I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven, and the first earth was gone
evidence.target: In the beginning GOD created heaven and earth

21:1.note: The last book answers the first in its own words: the heaven and earth created in the beginning give place to a new heaven and a new earth.

evidence.source: no curse shall be any more
evidence.target: cursed is the earth in thy work: with much toiling shalt thou eat thereof

22:3.note: The end answers the beginning: in the city of God no curse shall be any more, where Eden heard the earth cursed in man's work.

evidence.source: that great dragon was cast forth, the old serpent, which is called the devil and Satan
evidence.target: the serpent also was more subtile than all the beasts of the earth

12:9.note: The Apocalypse names Eden's serpent outright: the old serpent, the devil and Satan, the seducer of the whole world.

evidence.source: death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying
evidence.target: in what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death

21:4.note: The death threatened at the tree, and entered by the eating of it, is abolished in the new creation: death shall be no more — the last word of the story answering the sentence of its first sin.

evidence.source: his kingdom was made dark
evidence.target: horrible darkness in the whole Land of Ægypt three days

16:10.note: The vial judgments replay the Egyptian plagues upon the beast's kingdom: the fifth vial's darkness, in which men gnaw their tongues, answers the ninth plague's three days of darkness over Egypt.

evidence.source: singing the song of Moyses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb
evidence.target: Then sang Moyses and the children of Israel this song to our Lord

15:3.note: The victors by the sea of glass sing 'the song of Moses the servant of God' — the song first sung on the far shore of the Red Sea — joined now to the song of the Lamb.

evidence.source: hath made us a Kingdom and Priests to God
evidence.target: you shall be unto me a Priestly Kingdom

1:6.note: What God promised Israel at Sinai — 'you shall be unto me a priestly kingdom' — John blesses Christ for having made of his redeemed: 'a kingdom and priests to God'.

evidence.source: Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them. And they shall be his people: and he God with them shall be their God
evidence.target: they shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of them

21:3.note: The promise first spoken for the tabernacle — 'I will dwell in the midst of them' — is the last word of the new creation, where the tabernacle of God is with men (John also gathers Leviticus 26 and Ezechiel 37 into it).

evidence.source: Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them. And they shall be his people: and he God with them shall be their God
evidence.target: I will walk among you, & will be your God, & you shall be my people

21:3.note: The covenant formula of Leviticus 26:12 reaches its last form in the new Jerusalem: God dwelling with men, they his people, he their God. Ezekiel 37:27 stands between (entered at 26:11).

evidence.source: them that hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a scandal before the children of Israel, to eat and commit fornication
evidence.target: that deceived the children of Israel at the suggestion of Balaam, and made you prevaricate against our Lord upon the sin of Phogor

2:14.note: Moses' own indictment names the teacher John condemns: the eating and fornication at Phogor were Balaam's suggestion. The seed keys this verse of John to Balaam's parting counsel (24:14) and to the sin itself (25:2), but not to the verse that names its author.

evidence.source: I beheld the earth, and lo it was void, and a thing of nothing: and the heavens, & there was no light in them
evidence.target: the earth was void and vacant, and darkness was upon the face of the depth

4:23.note: Jeremias sees judgment as un-creation: the earth void again as before the first day, and the heavens without the light God made.

evidence.source: the mourning, and weeping of Rachel weeping for her children
evidence.target: Rachel therefore died, and was buried in the high way that leadeth to Ephrata

31:15.note: Rachel weeps in Jeremias from the grave Genesis records for her, on the high way that leadeth to Ephrata — the Bethlehem road.

evidence.source: You have not heard me, to proclaim liberty every man to his brother, and every one to his friend
evidence.target: shalt proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land

34:17.note: Jerusalem's masters made the jubilee proclamation — liberty to their Hebrew slaves — and then took it back. Jeremiah answers with God's counter-proclamation of 'liberty' to the sword, the pestilence and the famine, turning Leviticus 25:10's word against them.

evidence.source: because there came a fire out of Hesebon, and a flame out of the midst of Sehon, and it hath devoured part of Moab, and the top of the children of tumult
evidence.target: Afire went forth from Hesebon, a flame from the town of Sehon, & devoured Ar of the Moabites, and the inhabitants of the high places of Arnon

48:45.note: Jeremiah takes up the ancient proverb of Hesebon and turns it on Moab itself: the fire that once went forth from Sehon's town for Israel now devours Moab's own children of tumult.

evidence.source: Woe to thee Moab, thou hast perished, o people of Chamos: because thy sons are taken, and thy daughters into captivity
evidence.target: Woe to thee Moab, thou art undone people of Chamos. He hath given his sons into flight, and his daughters into captivity to Sehon the King of the Amorrheites

48:46.note: The proverb's woe over Moab stands word for word in Jeremiah's mouth; only the flight of the sons has ripened into captivity.

evidence.source: the Heavens were before, and the earth, out of water, and through water, consisting by the word of God
evidence.target: the Spirit of God moved over the waters

3:5.note: Peter's scoffers wilfully forget the first world as Genesis shews it: earth consisting out of water and through water, by the word of God.

evidence.source: that world then, being overflowed with water perished
evidence.target: all flesh was consumed that moved upon the earth

3:6.note: The world that then perished, overflowed with water, is the flood of Genesis, when all flesh that moved upon the earth was consumed.

evidence.source: having followed the way of Balaam of Bosor, which loved the reward of iniquity
evidence.target: having the price of divination in their hands

2:15.note: The reward Balaam loved is here in the elders' hands — the price of divination carried out to him. The 'way' Peter names is the road the angel meets at 22:32 ('thy way is perverse'). The seed carries Peter's next verse, the speaking ass, at 22:23.

evidence.source: gathering the fowls of the heaven, and fishes of the sea
evidence.target: rule over the fishes and the sea, and fowls of the air

1:3.note: Sophonias' gathering-away of man, beast, fowl, and fish unmakes the order of Genesis 1 in reverse: judgment as de-creation.

evidence.source: we clay: and thou art our maker, and all we the works of thy hands
evidence.target: formed man of the slime of the earth

64:8.note: Isaiah's prayer takes its plea from the making of Adam: we are the clay, and the God who formed man of the slime of the earth is our maker and father.

evidence.source: his rod upon the sea, and he shall lift it up in the way of Ægypt
evidence.target: lift up thy rod, and stretch forth thy hand upon the sea, and divide it

10:26.note: Isaias threatens Assyria with the rod lifted over the sea 'in the way of Egypt' — Moses' rod, stretched out to divide the waters.

evidence.source: there shall be a way to the remnant of my people, which shall be left of the Assyrians: as there was to Israel in the day, that he came up out of the Land of Ægypt
evidence.target: went through the midst of the dry sea

11:16.note: The remnant's highway out of Assyria is promised in Exodus' own terms: a way through the sea 'as there was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt'.

evidence.source: Which brought forth the chariot & the horse, the arm and the strong: they slept together, neither shall they rise again
evidence.target: the waters returned, and overwhelmed the chariots & the horsemen of all Pharao's army, who following were entered into the sea, neither did there so much as one of them remain

43:17.note: Isaias' new-Exodus song names the drowned host exactly as Exodus does: chariot and horse, and not one of them remaining.

evidence.source: and our Lord hath put upon him the iniquity of all us
evidence.target: let him confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their offences and sins: which praying to light on his head

53:6.note: All Israel's iniquities, confessed over the goat's head to light on him and be carried away — Isaiah sees that laying-on concentrated on the Servant: the Lord 'put upon him the iniquity of all us'.

evidence.source: the same my just servant shall justify many, and he shall bear their iniquities
evidence.target: And when the goat hath carried all their iniquities into the solitary ground

53:11.note: 'He shall bear their iniquities' — the scapegoat's work, carrying all the iniquities away into the solitary ground, becomes the Servant's own bearing. 1 Peter 2:24 takes the line up from Isaiah and is set aside here as mediated.

evidence.source: Is this such a fast, as I have chosen: for a man by the day to afflict his soul?
evidence.target: The seventh month, the tenth day of the month you shall afflict your souls

58:5.note: Isaiah's question is aimed at the Day of Atonement's own phrase — 'afflict your souls', the one commanded soul-affliction of the year. The prophet asks whether bowing the head like a rush is the affliction God chose.

evidence.source: preach indulgence to the captives, and deliverance to them that are shut up
evidence.target: Thou shalt sanctify the fiftieth year, and shalt proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land: for it is the year of Jubilee

61:1.note: The anointed one's proclamation to captives is the jubilee act itself: in the fiftieth year remission is proclaimed to all the land's inhabitants, and every man returns to his possession. Jesus reads this text at Nazareth (Luke 4) — that link runs through Isaiah and is set aside as mediated.

evidence.source: they that did eat swine's flesh, and abomination, and the mouse
evidence.target: the swine: which though it divideth the hoof, cheweth not the cud

66:17.note: Isaiah's condemned garden-rites feast on Leviticus 11's own unclean list — the swine named at 11:7, the mouse following at 11:29 among the creeping things.

evidence.source: he is a liar, & the father thereof
evidence.target: the serpent said to the woman: No, you shall not die the death

8:44.note: The devil is a liar and the father of lies; his first recorded lie is the flat denial of God's word in Eden: No, you shall not die the death.

evidence.source: before that Abraham was made, I am
evidence.target: I am Which AM

8:58.note: 'Before Abraham was made, I am': the Lord takes to himself the Name spoken at the bush, I AM.

evidence.source: Your fathers did eat Manna in the desert; and they died
evidence.target: This is the bread, which our Lord hath given you to eat

6:49.note: 'Your fathers did eat manna in the desert, and they died': the Lord sets the gift of Exodus — 'this is the bread which our Lord hath given you' — against the bread that does not let men die.

evidence.source: God no man hath seen at any time
evidence.target: Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me, & live

1:18.note: 'God no man hath seen at any time' stands on the word spoken to Moses: 'man shall not see me, and live' — which is why the only-begotten Son, not a vision, is the declaration of the Father.

evidence.source: God sent his Son made of a woman, made under the Law
evidence.target: I will put enmity between thee & the woman, & thy seed and the seed of her

4:4.note: The promise in Eden ran between the serpent and the woman, her seed against his: in the fullness of time God sent his Son made of a woman, the woman's seed come to end the enmity.

evidence.source: on the Gentiles the blessing of Abraham might be made in Christ Jesus
evidence.target: IN Thee shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed

3:14.note: Paul names the blessing of Abraham made upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus: the kindreds of the earth blessed in Abraham, as was promised.

evidence.source: which is Agar
evidence.target: having an handmaid, an Ægyptian named Agar

4:24.note: Paul's allegory takes its figure from Genesis' plain introduction: Sarai's Egyptian handmaid, named Agar.

evidence.source: are the two testaments. The one from mount Sina, gendering unto bondage; which is Agar
evidence.target: our Lord descended upon the mount Sinai

4:24.note: Paul's allegory of the two covenants turns entirely on Sinai as the mountain where the covenant 'gendering unto bondage' was given — the descent of the Lord upon the mount in Exodus 19.

evidence.source: we brethren, according to Isaac, are the children of promise
evidence.target: she conceived & bare a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold her

4:28.note: To be children of promise 'according to Isaac' is to be born as Isaac was: by promise, at the time God foretold, to parents in their old age.

evidence.source: the Law which was made after four hundred and thirty years
evidence.target: that they abode in Ægypt, was four hundred thirty years

3:17.note: Paul's whole argument from chronology hangs on Exodus' own figure: the sojourn was four hundred thirty years, and the Law came after.

evidence.source: all that take the sword shall perish with the sword
evidence.target: Whosoever shall shed man's blood, his blood shall be shed: for to the image of God man was made

26:52.note: The Lord's word in Gethsemane restates the flood covenant's law: blood for blood, and its reason — man made to the image of God.

evidence.source: Judas begat Phares and Zaram of Thamar
evidence.target: the other came forth: and the woman said: Why is the partition divided for thee? And for this cause called his name Phares

1:3.note: Matthew's genealogy keeps Thamar and her twins in the royal line: Phares, named for the partition divided at his birth.

evidence.source: they are dead that sought the life of the child
evidence.target: they are all dead that sought thy life

2:20.note: The angel's word to Joseph repeats, nearly word for word, God's word to Moses in Madian; Matthew draws the parallel between the two children himself.

evidence.source: He that shall curse father or mother, dying let him die
evidence.target: He that curseth his father, or mother, dying let him die

15:4.note: The Lord quotes the law of the cursing child in its own words, beside the fifth commandment (which the seed already carries at 20:12).

evidence.source: there came they that received the didrachmes
evidence.target: half a sicle according to the measure of the temple. A sicle hath twenty oboles. The half part of a sicle shall be offered to the Lord

17:23.note: The didrachma the collectors seek from the Lord is the half-shekel first imposed at the numbering in Exodus — every man's ransom 'offered to the Lord'; the Lord's answer turns on who truly owes it. (In this corpus the collectors' question stands at Matthew 17:23.)

evidence.source: You have heard that it was said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.
evidence.target: eye for eye, tooth for tooth he shall restore

5:38.note: The Lord quotes the talion clause of Leviticus 24 — the law of retaliation that follows the blasphemer's case — before his own 'But I say to you not to resist evil'.

evidence.source: Again you have heard that it was said to them of old, Thou shalt not commit perjury: but thou shall perform thy oaths to our Lord.
evidence.target: Thou shalt not forswear thyself in my name, nor pollute the name of thy God

5:34.note: The old saying the Lord cites is Leviticus' ban on swearing falsely by God's name; its second half also gathers the law of vows performed (Numbers 30). In this corpus the oath saying stands at Matthew 5:34; the seed keys that verse to the neighbouring 19:11, but the perjury clause itself is 19:12.

evidence.source: but thou shall perform thy oaths to our Lord
evidence.target: all that he promised he shall fulfill

5:34.note: The second half of the old saying in the Sermon — perform thy oaths to the Lord — is the vow law of this verse. Its perjury half is already keyed to Leviticus 19:12 in our layer; in this corpus the saying stands at Matthew 5:34.

evidence.source: I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us if thou be Christ the Son of God
evidence.target: If a soul sin, and hear the voice of one swearing, and be witness, because either he himself saw, or is privy to it: unless he utter it, he shall bear his iniquity

26:63.note: Caiaphas puts Jesus under adjuration — the solemn 'voice of one swearing' of Leviticus 5:1, which binds the hearer who is privy to the matter to utter it or bear his iniquity. Jesus, who had held his peace, answers under it.

evidence.source: Then the high Priest rent his garments, saying: He hath blasphemed
evidence.target: he shall not rent his garments

26:65.note: At the verdict the high priest does the one thing Leviticus forbids the anointed high priest to do, even in mourning: he rents his garments.

evidence.source: For we have seen his star in the East, and are come to adore him.
evidence.target: A star Shall Rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel

2:2.note: The star the Sages follow to Bethlehem is Balaam's star, risen out of Jacob in the last of his parables. Our Genesis stage already keys Jacob's own blessing (Gen 49:10) to this verse; the sighting itself was still unkeyed.

evidence.source: And seeing the multitudes, he pitied them; because they were vexed, and lay like sheep that have not a shepherd
evidence.target: lest the people of our Lord be as sheep without a pastor

9:36.note: The compassion of Jesus over the multitudes speaks Moses' prayer back to him — sheep without a shepherd — and answers it in his own person, the man provided to go in and out before them.

evidence.source: he made of one, all mankind, to inhabit upon the whole face of the earth
evidence.target: of these was all mankind spread over the whole earth

17:26.note: Paul at Athens teaches Genesis 9: of Noe's three sons was all mankind spread over the whole earth.

evidence.source: every man heard them speak in his own tongue
evidence.target: let us go down, and there confound their tongue, that none may hear his neighbour's voice

2:6.note: Pentecost is Babel answered: there the tongue was confounded so that none might hear his neighbour's voice; here every man hears the great works of God in his own tongue.

evidence.source: called thither Jacob his father and all his kindred in seventy five souls
evidence.target: All the souls of the house of Jacob, that entered into Ægypt, were seventy

7:14.note: Stephen reckons the kindred at seventy-five souls, following the Greek reckoning; Genesis as here printed numbers the house that entered Egypt at seventy.

evidence.source: called thither Jacob his father and all his kindred in seventy five souls
evidence.target: all the souls that came out of Jacob's thigh were seventy

7:14.note: Stephen counts the kindred at seventy-five souls, following the Greek reckoning; Exodus counts seventy. The difference is printed openly in both texts, not smoothed over.

evidence.source: another king arose in Ægypt, that knew not Joseph
evidence.target: there arose a new king over Ægypt, that knew not Joseph

7:18.note: Stephen's history begins where Exodus begins: a new king in Egypt who did not know Joseph.

evidence.source: Pharao's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son
evidence.target: Whom she adopted into the place of a son

7:21.note: Stephen: Pharaoh's daughter took the exposed child up and nourished him as her own son; Exodus: she adopted him into the place of a son.

evidence.source: Who hath appointed thee prince and judge over us
evidence.target: Who hath appointed thee Prince and Judge over us?

7:27.note: Stephen quotes the Hebrew workman's rebuff of Moses word for word.

evidence.source: whom they denied, saying: Who hath appointed thee prince and Captain?
evidence.target: Who hath appointed thee Prince and Judge over us?

7:35.note: Stephen re-deploys the question against his hearers: the Moses they denied with these words is the one God sent as prince and redeemer. The Acts text here prints 'Captain' where 7:27 has 'judge'.

evidence.source: Moyses fled upon this word: and he became a sojourner in the land of Madian
evidence.target: who flying from his sight, abode in the Land of Madian

7:29.note: Moses' flight from Pharaoh's sight and his sojourning in Madian, retold by Stephen.

evidence.source: Loose off the shoe of thy feet, for the place wherein thou standest, is holy ground
evidence.target: loose off thy shoe from thy feet: for the place wherein thou standest is holy ground

7:33.note: Stephen quotes the word at the bush: the shoe loosed, the ground holy.

evidence.source: I am the God of thy fathers; the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob
evidence.target: I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob

7:32.note: Stephen quotes God's self-naming at the bush, 'thy fathers' for Exodus' 'thy father'.

evidence.source: Seeing I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Ægypt, and I have heard their groaning
evidence.target: I have seen the affliction of my people in Ægypt, and I have heard their cry

7:34.note: Stephen quotes the opening of the call: God has seen the affliction and heard the cry (his 'descended to deliver' is 3:8).

evidence.source: And now come, and I will send thee into Ægypt
evidence.target: come, and I will send thee to Pharao

7:34.note: The same verse of Stephen quotes the commission itself: 'come, and I will send thee' — in Exodus, to Pharaoh; in Stephen's retelling, into Egypt.

evidence.source: in a mighty arm brought them out thereof
evidence.target: redeem you in a high arm, and great judgments

13:17.note: Paul at Antioch: God brought Israel out 'in a mighty arm' — Exodus' own word for the redemption, 'in a high arm, and great judgments'.

evidence.source: they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice to the idol
evidence.target: made of them a molten calf. And they said: These are thy gods Israel

7:41.note: Stephen's indictment: in those days they made the calf and offered sacrifice to the idol, as Exodus tells it.

evidence.source: for I did never eat any common and unclean thing
evidence.target: that you may know the differences of the clean, and the unclean, and know what you ought to eat, and what to refuse

10:14.note: Peter's protest is spoken out of Leviticus 11, whose own closing verse states the code's purpose — to know what to eat and what to refuse. The vision answers the code at its summary verse.

evidence.source: That you abstain from the things immolated to idols, and blood, and that which is strangled
evidence.target: Any man whosoever of the house of Israel, and of the strangers, that sojourn among them, if he eat blood, I will set my face against his life

15:29.note: The apostolic decree's blood clause rests on the one blood law in Leviticus that expressly names the sojourning stranger — the ground on which it can bind Gentile believers, whose meat (like the strangled) kept its blood.

evidence.source: a certain wench having a Pythonical spirit, met us, that brought great gain to her masters by divining
evidence.target: Man, or woman, in whom is a pythonical or divining spirit

16:16.note: This translation uses the same rare word in both places: the Philippian girl's 'Pythonical spirit' is the very thing Leviticus 20:27 names — and Paul expels it rather than profit by it. Saul's errand at 1 Kings 28:7 uses the same word (entered separately).

evidence.source: whereas now it was not safe sailing, because the fast now was past
evidence.target: upon the tenth day of this seventh month shall be the day of expiations most solemn

27:9.note: Luke dates the voyage by 'the fast' without explaining it — his readers know the one fast of the year, the Day of Expiations on the tenth day of the seventh month.

evidence.source: And when the days of Pentecost were accomplished, they were all together in one place
evidence.target: unto the morrow after the seventh week be expired, that is to say fifty days, and so you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord

2:1.note: Pentecost is Leviticus' fiftieth day, counted out from the firstfruits sheaf. The Spirit falls on the feast's own day — the church is gathered at the hour the law's count appointed.

evidence.source: it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in that day, than for that city
evidence.target: rained upon Sodome and Gomorre brimstone & fire from our Lord out of heaven

10:12.note: The Lord makes Sodom — the city rained on with fire — the measure of tolerableness in the day of judgment.

evidence.source: he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people
evidence.target: Visiting I have visited you: and I have seen all things that have chanced to you in Ægypt

1:68.note: In Exodus, God's 'visiting' his people is their redemption out of Egypt; Zacharias blesses the same visitation come again: he 'hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people'.

evidence.source: if I in the finger of God
evidence.target: This is the finger of God

11:20.note: The magicians' confession over the plagues — 'This is the finger of God' — is the phrase the Lord takes up for his casting out of devils.

evidence.source: they told his decease that he should accomplish in Jerusalem
evidence.target: it is the Phase (that is the Passage) of the Lord

9:31.note: On the mountain Moses himself, with Elias, speaks with Jesus of his 'decease' — in the Greek, his exodus — to be accomplished in Jerusalem: the Lord's death named as the true Passage, of which the paschal night was the figure.

evidence.source: Do this for a commemoration of me
evidence.target: you shall have this day for a monument: & you shall celebrate it solemn to the Lord

22:19.note: The Lord institutes his own memorial at the Passover table: 'Do this for a commemoration of me' answers the day Exodus appointed to be kept 'for a monument' in every generation.

evidence.source: Let your loins be girded
evidence.target: You shall gird your reins, and you shall have shoes on your feet, holding staves in your hands, and you shall eat speedily

12:35.note: The watchful servants of the parable wear the Passover's own posture — loins girt, in the night, ready for the Lord's coming.

evidence.source: And after eight days were expired, that the child should be circumcised
evidence.target: And the eighth day the little infant shall be circumcised

2:21.note: The child is circumcised on Leviticus' day, within the mother's purification days. Genesis 17 commands the rite itself; John 7:22's sabbath argument from this verse is seed-carried.

evidence.source: Thou hast answered right, this do and thou shalt live
evidence.target: which a man doing, shall live in them

10:28.note: Jesus seals the lawyer's answer with Leviticus' own promise in short form — do, and live. Paul quotes the full clause at Romans 10:5 (seed-carried).

evidence.source: If thy brother sin against thee, rebuke him: and if he do penance, forgive him
evidence.target: Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart, but control him openly, lest thou incur sin through him

17:3.note: 'Rebuke him' is Leviticus' open reproof — the appointed alternative to nursing hatred of a brother in the heart. The Lord joins to it the forgiveness Leviticus leaves implicit.

evidence.source: and lifting up his hands he blessed them
evidence.target: And stretching forth his hand to the people, he blessed them

24:50.note: The departing Lord takes Aaron's stance at his first blessing — hands lifted over the disciples as he is parted from them. Sirach's Simon does the same at the altar (entered as allusion).

evidence.source: to whom thou swarest by thine own self, saying: I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven
evidence.target: I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven, and as the sand that is by the sea shore

32:13.note: Moses intercedes by pleading the sworn promise back to God: the stars of heaven, in the oath's own words.

evidence.source: Our Lord make this woman, which entereth into thy house, as Rachel, and Lia, which builded the house of Israel
evidence.target: opened her womb, her sister remaining barren

4:11.note: Bethlehem's elders bless Ruth in the names of Rachel and Lia, the two mothers who builded the house of Israel out of barren and opened wombs.

evidence.source: thy house may be, as the house of Phares, whom Thamar bare to Judas
evidence.target: for this cause called his name Phares

4:12.note: The blessing on Booz's house names its own ancestor: Phares, whom Thamar bare to Judas, named for the breach at his birth.

evidence.source: He turned their heart that they hated his people: and to work guile toward his servants
evidence.target: Come, let us wisely oppress the same, lest perhaps it multiply

104:25.note: The psalm reads Egypt's oppression as God's turning of their heart; its 'work guile' answers the king's 'let us wisely oppress' — the same craft, seen from heaven's side.

evidence.source: he brought them forth with gold and silver
evidence.target: they asked of the Ægyptians vessels of silver and gold

104:37.note: The psalm's Exodus litany: God brought Israel forth laden with the silver and gold they had asked of the Egyptians.

evidence.source: they believed his words: and they sang his praises
evidence.target: the people feared our Lord, and they believed our Lord, and Moyses his servant

105:12.note: The psalm compresses the shore of the sea into one line: they believed — as Exodus says, 'the people feared our Lord, and they believed' — and then they sang.

evidence.source: Our Lord is my strength, and my praise: and he is made my salvation
evidence.target: My strength, and my praise is our Lord, and he is made unto me a salvation

117:14.note: The Hallel psalm takes the song of Moses for its own line, word for word with only the order turned.

evidence.source: The right hand of our Lord hath wrought strength
evidence.target: Thy right hand, o Lord, is magnified in strength

117:16.note: The same psalm's triple 'the right hand of our Lord' answers the song's 'Thy right hand, o Lord, is magnified in strength'.

evidence.source: he brought them into the mount of his sanctification
evidence.target: bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thy inheritance, in thy most firm habitation, which thou hast wrought, o Lord: thy sanctuary Lord, which thy hands have confirmed

77:54.note: The psalm's history ends where the song pointed: God bringing his people in and planting them in the mountain of his sanctuary.

evidence.source: And he rained them Manna to eat, and bread of heaven he gave to them
evidence.target: Behold I will rain you bread from heaven

77:24.note: The psalm takes God's verb for its own: as God said 'I will rain you bread from heaven', so 'he rained them manna to eat'.

evidence.source: As in the provocation according to the day of the tentation in the desert: where your fathers tempted me
evidence.target: he called the name of that place, Temptation, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and for that they tempted our Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?

94:9.note: The psalm's 'day of temptation in the desert' is the place Exodus itself names Temptation — Massa — where Israel said, 'Is the Lord among us or not?'

evidence.source: they made a calf in Horeb: and they adored the sculptile
evidence.target: he formed them by founder's work, and made of them a molten calf

105:19.note: The psalm of Israel's rebellions: 'they made a calf in Horeb, and they adored the sculptile' — Aaron's molten calf of Exodus 32.

evidence.source: Our Lord is pitiful, and merciful: long suffering, and very merciful
evidence.target: merciful and clement, patient and of much compassion

102:8.note: The psalm of thanksgiving opens its praise with the Sinai formula: 'Our Lord is pitiful and merciful, long suffering and very merciful'.

evidence.source: That hath not given his money to usury, and hath not taken gifts upon the innocent
evidence.target: Thou shalt not give him thy money to usury, and an overplus of the fruits thou shalt not exact of him

14:5.note: The entrance psalm's righteous man is drawn with Leviticus' usury clause — he 'hath not given his money to usury' to his brother. (Psalm 14 in the Vulgate numbering this corpus uses; 15 in modern Bibles.)

evidence.source: Sound ye with trumpet in the new moon, in the notable day of your solemnity.
evidence.target: The seventh month, on the first day of the month, shall be a Sabbath, a memorial, by sounding of trumpets

80:4.note: The psalm summons the trumpet for the appointed solemnity at the new moon — the memorial of blowing trumpets on the first day of the seventh month, which opens the autumn feasts of Leviticus 23.

evidence.source: And these have not known my ways: as I sware in my wrath: if they shall enter into my rest
evidence.target: they shall not see the Land for the which I sware to their fathers, neither shall any of them that hath detracted me, behold it

94:11.note: The oath the psalm sings — the text Hebrews 3-4 preaches — was sworn here, at Cades, against the generation of the spies: they shall not see the land.

evidence.source: And they coveted concupiscence in the desert: and tempted God in the place without water
evidence.target: For the common vulgar people that came up with them, burned with desire, sitting and weeping, the children of Israel being joined together with them

105:14.note: The psalm's 'concupiscence in the desert' is this burning desire for flesh — the craving that named the place itself, the Sepulchres of concupiscence (11:34). Paul's 'as they also coveted' is seed-carried at this verse.

evidence.source: And he rained upon them flesh as dust: and as the sand of the sea feathered fowls
evidence.target: And a wind coming forth from our Lord, taking quails over the sea brought them, and let them fall into the camp the space of one day's journey

77:27.note: The psalm's rain of flesh is this wind from the Lord, driving the quails in over the sea to fall around the camp. Wisdom's retelling of the quails is already keyed to this verse in our layer.

evidence.source: They were not defrauded of their desire. As yet their meats were in their mouth
evidence.target: As yet the flesh was in their teeth, neither had that kind of meat failed: & behold the fury of our Lord being provoked against the people, struck them with an exceeding great plague

77:30.note: Meats in the mouth, flesh in the teeth, and the blow falling while they ate — the psalm keeps Numbers' very image of the plague at the Sepulchres of concupiscence.

evidence.source: The earth was opened, and swallowed Dathan, and overwhelmed the congregation of Abiron
evidence.target: and opening her mouth, devoured them with their tabernacles & all their substance

105:17.note: The psalm's history names what this verse records: Dathan swallowed, Abiron's congregation overwhelmed, in the one opening of the earth.

evidence.source: And a fire flamed up in their synagogue: the flame burnt the sinners
evidence.target: But a fire also coming forth from our Lord, slew the two hundred fifty men, that offered the incense

105:18.note: The fire that flamed in their synagogue is the fire that took the two hundred fifty censer-bearers. Sirach's praise of Aaron reaches the same verse from the other side in our layer.

evidence.source: And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction: and Moyses was vexed for them
evidence.target: This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarrelled against our Lord, and he was sanctified in them

105:32.note: The psalm calls the place by the very name this verse gives it — the water of contradiction at Cades.

evidence.source: because they exasperated his spirit. And he plainly affirmed in his lips
evidence.target: Hear ye rebellious & incredulous: Can we out of this rock bring you forth water?

105:33.note: The psalm's diagnosis — a spirit exasperated, a rash word on the lips — is this cry before the rock, the word for which Moses lost the land he was not to enter.

evidence.source: God have mercy upon us, and bless us: illuminate his countenance upon us, and have mercy on us
evidence.target: Our Lord shew his face to thee, and have mercy upon thee

66:2.note: The psalm prays Aaron's blessing back upon the whole congregation — bless us, shew thy face on us, have mercy — in the blessing's own words and order.

evidence.source: The light of thy countenance, o Lord is signed upon us: thou hast given gladness in my heart
evidence.target: Our Lord turn his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace

4:7.note: The countenance lifted and turned upon the blessed one, and its fruit in the heart — gladness answering to the blessing's peace.

evidence.source: Let God arise, and let his enemies be dispersed, and let them that hate him fly from his face
evidence.target: Arise Lord, and be thine enemies dispersed, and let them fly that hate thee, from thy face

67:2.note: The psalm opens with Moses' cry at the rising of the ark, transposed into the third person for the liturgy — enemies dispersed, haters fled from his face — but the words are the ark's own.

evidence.source: Sehon the king of the Amorrheites: because his mercy is for ever
evidence.target: Of whom he was strucken in the edge of the sword, and his land was possessed from Arnon unto Jeboc

135:19.note: The litany's first conquered king is Sehon, struck in the edge of the sword at Jasa and possessed from Arnon to Jeboc. The seed points the sister psalm (134:11) at this chapter only.

evidence.source: And Og the king of Basan: because his mercy is for ever
evidence.target: Fear him not, for into thy hand I have delivered him, and all his people, and land: and thou shalt do to him as thou didst to Sehon the king of the Amorrheites, the inhabiter of Hesebon

135:20.note: The litany's second king is Og of Basan, delivered into Israel's hand by this word — do to him as thou didst to Sehon.

evidence.source: And Phinees stood, and pacified: and the slaughter ceased
evidence.target: And the plague ceased from the children of Israel

105:30.note: Phinees standing, and the plague ceasing — the psalm compresses the deed at the brothel house into its one effect, and the next verse reckons it to him for justice.

evidence.source: And it was reputed to him unto justice, in generation and generation even for ever
evidence.target: and there shall be as well to him as to his seed the covenant of priesthood for ever, because he hath been zealous for his God, and hath expiated the wicked fact of the children of Israel

105:31.note: The psalm reckons Phinees' zeal with Abraham's own reckoning word — reputed unto justice — and its 'for ever' is this covenant's: an everlasting priesthood to him and to his seed. Sirach's praise of Phinees is keyed to the same verse in our layer.

evidence.source: brought out of the iron furnace of Ægypt
evidence.target: the hard works of clay and brick

4:20.note: Deuteronomy's 'iron furnace of Egypt' is the brick-kiln bondage of Exodus 1 named in a single image.

evidence.source: The blessing of him, that appeared in the bush
evidence.target: appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush

33:16.note: In Moses' blessing of Joseph, God is named simply as him 'that appeared in the bush' — the theophany of Exodus 3 become one of his titles.

evidence.source: thou shalt bind them as a sign on thy hand, and they shall be and shall move between thine eyes
evidence.target: it shall be as a sign in thy hand, and as a monument before thine eyes

6:8.note: The sign upon the hand and the monument before the eyes were first appointed for the memorial of the Exodus; Deuteronomy binds the words of the Law itself with the same sign.

evidence.source: and fed thee with Manna in the wilderness, which thy fathers knew not
evidence.target: Man-hu! Which signifieth: What is this! For they knew not what it was

8:16.note: Deuteronomy's recital: God fed Israel 'with manna, which thy fathers knew not' — Exodus records the not-knowing itself: 'Man-hu — what is this? for they knew not what it was'.

evidence.source: who brought forth rivers out of the hardest rock
evidence.target: thou shalt strike the rock, & water shall go out thereof

8:15.note: Deuteronomy's recital of the wilderness: God 'brought forth rivers out of the hardest rock' — the rock of Horeb, struck at God's command.

evidence.source: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God, as thou didst tempt him in the place of tentation
evidence.target: he called the name of that place, Temptation

6:16.note: 'Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God, as thou didst tempt him in the place of temptation' — Deuteronomy turns the named place of Exodus 17 into a standing commandment.

evidence.source: thou shalt destroy his name under heaven
evidence.target: I will destroy the memory of Amalec from under heaven

25:19.note: The blot-out command is repeated at the end of the Law in nearly Exodus' words: what God swore at Rephidim, Israel is charged to perform in the land.

evidence.source: Give from among you wise and skillful men, and such whose conversation is approved in your tribes, that I may appoint them your princes
evidence.target: provide out of all the people men that are wise, & do fear God, in whom there is truth, and that do hate avarice, and appoint of them tribunes, and centurions

1:13.note: Moses' own retelling of the appointment of rulers: the wise men of Jethro's counsel become, in Deuteronomy, the heads chosen from the tribes.

evidence.source: hath he spread his wings, and he hath taken him, and carried him on his shoulders
evidence.target: I have carried you upon the wings of eagles

32:11.note: The Song of Moses takes up God's Sinai word and makes it a picture: as the eagle carries her young, 'I have carried you upon the wings of eagles'.

evidence.source: I the Lord thy God, that brought thee out of the Land of Ægypt out of the house of servitude
evidence.target: which brought thee forth out of the Land of Ægypt, out of the house of servitude

5:6.note: Deuteronomy 5 repeats the Decalogue of Exodus 20 entire, on the plains of Moab a generation later; the preface stands word for word at the head of both givings.

evidence.source: as thou didst request of our Lord thy God in Horeb, when the assembly was gathered, and saidst: I will no more hear the voice of our Lord my God, and this exceeding great fire I will see no more, lest I die
evidence.target: let not our Lord Speak to us, lest perhaps we die

18:16.note: The promise of the prophet is grounded in Israel's plea at Horeb: 'let not our Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die' — Deuteronomy quotes the plea back as the reason God will speak through a mediator.

evidence.source: And do you therefore love strangers because you also were strangers in the Land of Ægypt
evidence.target: for you know the hearts of strangers: because yourselves also were strangers in the Land of Ægypt

10:19.note: The motive is Exodus' own, repeated verbatim: love the stranger, 'because yourselves also were strangers in the land of Egypt'.

evidence.source: two tables of stone written with the finger of God
evidence.target: two stone tables of testimony, written with the finger of God

9:10.note: Moses' retelling keeps the phrase entire: the tables were 'written with the finger of God' (the gift itself is Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:16 says the same of the first tables).

evidence.source: I cast the tables out of my hands, and brake them in your sight
evidence.target: he threw the tables out of his hand, and brake them at the foot of the mount

9:17.note: Moses' own retelling of the breaking of the tables at the foot of the mount.

evidence.source: your sin that you had committed, that is, the calf, I took, and burnt it with fire, and breaking it into pieces, and bringing it wholly into dust, I threw it into the torrent
evidence.target: he burnt it, & beat it into powder, which he strawed into water, and gave thereof drink to the children of Israel

9:21.note: The calf's destruction retold by Moses: burnt, ground to powder, and strawed on water — in Exodus, water the children of Israel were made to drink.

evidence.source: He that said to his father and to his mother: I know you not; and to his brethren: I know you not
evidence.target: every man kill his brother, and friend, and neighbour

33:9.note: Levi's blessing is the wage of the calf: the Levites who, at Moses' word, knew neither brother nor friend nor neighbour are blessed as the tribe that 'said to his father and mother, I know you not'.

evidence.source: there rose no more a Prophet in Israel as Moyses, whom our Lord had known face to face
evidence.target: spake unto Moyses face to face

34:10.note: The epitaph of Moses measures all prophecy after him by Exodus' word: the Lord knew him 'face to face'.

evidence.source: Hew thee two tables of stones, as the former were
evidence.target: Cut thee two tables of stone like unto the former

10:1.note: The second tables in Moses' retelling: 'hew thee two tables of stones, as the former were', as God commanded after the breaking.

evidence.source: thou shalt not return to take it away: but thou shalt suffer the stranger, and the pupil, and the widow to take it away
evidence.target: neither shalt thou gather the ears that remain

24:19.note: Deuteronomy re-legislates Leviticus' gleaning law as the forgotten sheaf: what the reaper leaves behind is suffered to the stranger, the pupil and the widow. Leviticus extends the same mercy to the vineyard at 19:10 — left 'to the poor, and the strangers to take'.

evidence.source: and because they hired against thee Balaam, the son of Beor of Mesopotamia in Syria, to curse thee
evidence.target: Come therefore, and curse this people, because it is mightier than I

23:4.note: The hiring Deuteronomy will not let Israel forget is Balac's summons itself, in its own words: come, and curse this people.

evidence.source: & our Lord thy God would not hear Balaam, and he turned his cursing into thy blessing, for that he loved thee
evidence.target: That thou shouldst curse mine enemies I called thee: and thou contrary wise blessest them

23:5.note: The turning of cursing into blessing that Deuteronomy preaches is Balac's complaint verbatim: called to curse, he blessed contrariwise.

evidence.source: There shall not any of the men of this wicked generation see the good Land, which by oath I promised to your fathers
evidence.target: they shall not see the Land for the which I sware to their fathers, neither shall any of them that hath detracted me, behold it

1:35.note: Moses' retelling forty years on keeps the oath's own frame — not see the land, sworn to the fathers — with Caleb's exception following in both tellings.

evidence.source: until all the generation of the men that were warriors was consumed out of the camp, as our Lord had sworn
evidence.target: In this wilderness shall your carcasses lie. All you that are numbered from twenty years & upward, and have murmured against me

2:14.note: Thirty-eight years from Cadesbarne to Zared, Deuteronomy looks back and finds this sentence spent to the last man, 'as our Lord had sworn'.

evidence.source: whom the earth opening her mouth swallowed up with their houses and tabernacles, and all their substance, which they had in the midst of Israel
evidence.target: and opening her mouth, devoured them with their tabernacles & all their substance

11:6.note: Deuteronomy's rehearsal for the children keeps the event's own words — the earth's mouth, the tabernacles, all their substance.

evidence.source: because you did prevaricate against me in the midst of the children of Israel at the Waters of contradiction in Cades of the desert of Sin: and you did not sanctify me among the children of Israel
evidence.target: Because you have not believed me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring in these peoples into the land, which I will give them

32:51.note: At the sentence of Moses' own death the charge is read back in its first words: you did not sanctify me at the waters of contradiction.

evidence.source: Remember what our Lord your God did to Mary, in the way when you came out of Ægypt
evidence.target: and behold Mary appeared white with leprosy as it were snow

24:9.note: The law of the leper in Deuteronomy is taught by a memory: what befell Mary in the way — white with leprosy as snow — for speaking against Moyses.

evidence.source: And you came to this place: and there came forth Sehon the king of Hesebon, and Og the king of Basan, meeting us to fight. And we struck them
evidence.target: Of whom he was strucken in the edge of the sword, and his land was possessed from Arnon unto Jeboc

29:7.note: The covenant renewal in the plains of Moab looks back one generation: both kings came forth to fight at the border, and both were struck — the first land Israel ever possessed.

evidence.source: And Josue the son of Nun was replenished with the spirit of wisdom, because Moyses did put his hands upon him
evidence.target: And imposing his hands on his head, he repeated all things that our Lord had commanded

34:9.note: The wisdom Josue is full of when Moses dies is traced by Deuteronomy's last page to this laying on of hands before Eleazar and all the assembly.

evidence.source: But that which is once gone out of thy lips, thou shalt observe, & shalt do as thou hast promised to our Lord thy God, & hast spoken with thy proper will and thine own mouth
evidence.target: If any man make a vow to our Lord, or bind himself by an oath: he shall not make his word frustrate, but all that he promised he shall fulfill

23:23.note: Deuteronomy restates the vow law first spoken to the princes of the tribes (30:2 in this corpus's numbering): what has gone out of the lips must be fulfilled, not made frustrate.

evidence.source: Thou shalt not pity him, & thou shalt take away the guilty blood out of Israel, that it may be well with thee
evidence.target: Pollute not the land of your habitation, which is polluted with the blood of innocents: neither can it otherwise be expiated, but by his blood, that sheddeth another man's blood

19:13.note: Deuteronomy's command to purge the guilty blood from Israel rests on this verse's doctrine, the Torah's fullest statement of it: a land polluted with blood is expiated no other way than by the blood of him who shed it.

evidence.source: out of Ægypt I called my son
evidence.target: My first-begotten son is Israel

11:1.note: God called Israel 'my first-begotten son' in Exodus; Osee looks back: 'out of Egypt I called my son'.

evidence.source: But I the Lord thy God out of the Land of Ægypt: and God beside me thou shalt not know, and there is no Saviour beside me
evidence.target: I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee forth out of the Land of Ægypt

13:4.note: Osee re-utters the Decalogue's preface as accusation: 'I the Lord thy God out of the land of Egypt — and God beside me thou shalt not know'.

evidence.source: but they have entered into Beelphegor, and are alienated into confusion, and are become abominable, as those things, which they loved
evidence.target: And Israel was professed to Beelphegor, and our Lord being angry

9:10.note: The prophet's one word for Israel's fall in the wilderness is this verse's: entered into, professed to, Beelphegor. The seed carries the psalm's witness (105:28) at this verse; Osee's is its own.

evidence.source: the precious blood as it were of an immaculate and unspotted Lamb, Christ
evidence.target: a lamb without spot, a male, of a year old

1:19.note: Christ is the 'immaculate and unspotted Lamb'; the paschal lamb of Exodus must be 'a lamb without spot'.

evidence.source: an elect generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation
evidence.target: you shall be unto me a Priestly Kingdom, and a holy nation

2:9.note: Peter transposes Sinai's 'priestly kingdom' into 'kingly priesthood' and keeps 'a holy nation' word for word; his 'people of purchase' carries on 19:5's peculiar people.

evidence.source: because it is written: You shall be holy, because I am holy
evidence.target: Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy

1:16.note: Peter cites the holiness command with 'it is written'. Leviticus speaks it three times (11:44; 19:2; 20:7); this is the form addressed to the whole assembly. The seed already carries Peter's quotation at 20:7.

evidence.source: but only stand confidently, & you shall see the help of our Lord over you
evidence.target: stand, and see the great wonders of our Lord

20:17.note: Jahaziel's word to Josaphat replays Moses' word at the sea: stand, fear not, and see what the Lord will do.

evidence.source: It shall not be you that shall fight
evidence.target: Our Lord will fight for you and you shall hold your peace

20:17.note: 'It shall not be you that shall fight' is Exodus' promise in other words: 'Our Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace'.

evidence.source: for all the days of the desolation she kept a Sabbath, till the seventy years were expired
evidence.target: Then shall the land take pleasure in her sabbaths all the days of her desolation

36:21.note: The Chronicler reads the seventy years of exile as Leviticus 26:34 fulfilled, and says so in Jeremiah's name: the land, emptied of its people, at last keeps the sabbaths they had withheld from her.

evidence.source: fire descended from heaven, and devoured the holocausts & victims: and the majesty of our Lord filled the house
evidence.target: a fire coming forth from our Lord, devoured the holocaust, and the fat that was upon the altar

7:1.note: Solomon's dedication is Leviticus 9 written large: fire descends and devours the offerings, and the majesty of the Lord fills the house, as at the tabernacle's first altar.

evidence.source: Ozias therefore the king was a leper until the day of his death, and he dwelt in a house apart full of the leprosy
evidence.target: he shall dwell alone without the camp

26:21.note: The leper king lives out the leper's sentence — cut off from the house of the Lord he had invaded, dwelling apart until his death — exactly as Leviticus 13:46 appoints for everyone the disease marks.

evidence.source: Counsel therefore being taken of the king and the Princes, and of all the assembly of Jerusalem, they decreed to make the Phase the second month
evidence.target: in the second month, the fourteenth day of the month at even: with azymes and wild lettuce shall they eat it

30:2.note: Ezechias' Passover is kept under this provision: the Phase of the second month, first given for the man unclean upon a soul or far off in his journey (9:10).

evidence.source: According to the days of thy coming forth out of the Land of Ægypt I will shew him marvels
evidence.target: terrible and laudable, doing marvels

7:15.note: God promises Micheas a repetition of the Exodus: 'according to the days of thy coming forth out of Egypt I will shew him marvels' — the song's God is 'doing marvels'.

evidence.source: What God is like to thee, which takest away iniquity
evidence.target: Who is like to thee among the strong, o Lord?

7:18.note: Micheas opens with the song's own question — 'Who is like to thee?' — and turns it from God's power against Egypt to his taking away of iniquity.

evidence.source: what Balaam the son of Beor answered him: from Setim even to Galgal, that thou mightest know the justices of our Lord
evidence.target: and taking up his parable, he said: From Aram hath Balac king of the Moabites brought me, from the mountains of the East

6:5.note: The answer God bids his people remember is the parables of chapters 23-24; this is their head, where Balaam owns that Balac brought him to curse.

evidence.source: Manna failed after they did eat of the corn of the Land
evidence.target: the children of Israel did eat Manna forty years, till they came into the habitable land

5:12.note: The manna that began in the desert fails at Gilgal, exactly where Exodus set its term: Israel ate it 'until they touched the borders of the land of Chanaan'.

evidence.source: as Moyses the servant of our Lord had commanded the children of Israel, and it is written in the volume of the law of Moyses: an Altar of unhewed stones which iron hath not touched
evidence.target: thou shalt not build it of hewed stones: for if thou lift up thy knife over it, it shall be polluted

8:31.note: Josue builds the altar on Ebal expressly 'as Moses had commanded... in the volume of the law' — the unhewed stones of Exodus' altar law, on which no iron has been lifted.

evidence.source: & I would not hear him, but contrarywise by him I blessed you, and delivered you out of his hand
evidence.target: That thou shouldst curse mine enemies I called thee: and thou contrary wise blessest them

24:10.note: Josue's farewell rehearses the same reversal, and keeps its key word: 'contrarywise' in both the complaint and the retelling.

evidence.source: Forty years old was I when Moyses the servant of our Lord sent me from Cadesbarne, to view the Land, & I reported to him that which to me seemed true
evidence.target: Send men that may view the Land of Chanaan, which I will give to the children of Israel, one of every tribe, of the Princes

14:7.note: Caleb, pleading for Hebron in his old age, names the errand that began with this command — sent from Cadesbarne to view the land.

evidence.source: Is it a small thing to you that you sinned in Beelphegor, and until this present day the spot of this abomination abideth in us? And many of the people fell dead
evidence.target: And Israel was professed to Beelphegor, and our Lord being angry

22:17.note: The tribes beyond Jordan are warned by the standing spot of Phogor: the sin that abides is this professing to Beelphegor, for which the many fell.

evidence.source: saying: Our Lord commanded by the hand of Moyses, that a possession should be given us in the midst of our brethren. And he gave them according to the commandment of our Lord a possession in the midst of their father's brethren
evidence.target: The daughters of Salphaad require a just thing: give them possession among their father's kin, and let them succeed him in the inheritance

17:4.note: In the dividing of the land the daughters plead the ruling itself, and Josue gives the possession 'according to the commandment of our Lord' — this commandment, spoken to Moyses at their first asking.

evidence.source: Separate the cities of the fugitives, of the which I spake to you by the hand of Moyses
evidence.target: determine what cities shall be for the succour of fugitives, that have not voluntarily shed blood

20:2.note: Josue separates the very cities God 'spake of by the hand of Moyses': the refuge law of this chapter put into possession, six cities among the Levites' forty-eight (35:6).

evidence.source: but they shall be a pit and a snare for you, and a stumbling block at your side, and stakes in your eyes, till he take you away and destroy you from his excellent Land
evidence.target: they that remain, shall be unto you as it were nails in your eyes, and spears in your sides, and they shall be your adversaries in the Land of your habitation

23:13.note: Josue's farewell takes up the warning spoken on the march: the nations left in the land as nails — stakes — in the eyes, and spears in the sides.

evidence.source: I have recounted whatsoever Amalec hath done to Israel: how he resisted them in the way when they came up out of Ægypt
evidence.target: I will destroy the memory of Amalec from under heaven

15:2.note: God's 'recounting' of Amalec to Saul is the oath written at Rephidim falling due: the memory of Amalec, sworn to be destroyed from under heaven, is now to be destroyed by Israel's king.

evidence.source: Seek me a woman that hath a pythonical spirit, and I will go to her, and will ask by her
evidence.target: Man, or woman, in whom is a pythonical or divining spirit

28:7.note: Saul, who had put away the diviners under this very law, goes by night to a woman 'that hath a pythonical spirit' — the law's own phrase for what he seeks.

evidence.source: but that which you owe render unto it for sin
evidence.target: he shall offer for his offence a ram without spot out of the flocks

6:3.note: Even the Philistines' diviners know an offended god is answered with the offence offering: they send golden emerods and mice 'for sin' beside the ark — Leviticus' asham imitated by Gentiles, restitution carried to the sanctuary.

evidence.source: for neither is he a man that he may repent
evidence.target: God is not as man, that he may lie, nor as the son of man, that he may be changed

15:29.note: Samuel's sentence over Saul is Balaam's confession turned to judgment: God is not as man, to lie or to repent of his word — so the kingdom is rent and not restored.

evidence.source: I will give him to our Lord all the days of his life, & the razor shall not come upon his head
evidence.target: a razor shall not pass over his head

1:11.note: Anna's vow for Samuel borrows the Nazarite's visible mark — the unshorn head of a child given to the Lord all the days of his life.

evidence.source: the word that I did covenant with you when you came out of the Land of Ægypt
evidence.target: If therefore you will hear my voice, and keep my covenant

2:6.note: Aggeus steadies the builders by 'the word that I did covenant with you when you came out of the land of Egypt' — the covenant whose terms are 'if you will hear my voice, and keep my covenant'.

evidence.source: If a man take sanctified flesh in the skirt of his garment, and touch with the skirt thereof bread, or broth, or wine, or oil, or any meat: shall it be sanctified?
evidence.target: Whatsoever shall touch the flesh thereof, shall be sanctified

2:13.note: Aggeus is sent to 'ask the priests the law': his test case probes Leviticus 6:27, where what touches the sin offering's flesh is sanctified. The priests rule that holiness does not travel at second hand — and the prophet turns the ruling on the people's works.

evidence.source: If one polluted on a soul touch any of all these, shall he be contaminated?
evidence.target: He that toucheth a thing unclean by occasion of that is dead

2:14.note: The second test case is Leviticus' corpse-uncleanness: defilement, unlike holiness, does spread by touch. The priests' 'He shall be contaminated' applies the law of Aaron's seed to the whole nation.

evidence.source: He that shall curse father or mother, dying let him die
evidence.target: He that curseth his father, or mother, dying let him die

7:10.note: Mark's form of the same quotation: 'He that shall curse father or mother, dying let him die'.

evidence.source: And a woman which was in an issue of blood twelve years
evidence.target: The woman that hath a flux of blood many days not in her menstrual time

5:25.note: The woman's twelve-year issue is the case Leviticus 15:25 governs — a flux beyond the menstrual time, unclean all the days she is subject to it. She reaches Jesus through the crowd the law would have kept her apart from.

evidence.source: as it were the form of the sapphire stone the similitude of a throne
evidence.target: under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone

1:26.note: On Sinai the elders saw under God's feet 'as it were a work of sapphire stone'; by the Chebar, Ezechiel sees the throne itself in the likeness of sapphire above the firmament.

evidence.source: my tabernacle shall be in them: & I will be their God, and they shall be my people
evidence.target: I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel & will be their God

37:27.note: Ezechiel's restoration promise re-utters the tabernacle's dedication word: 'I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel, and will be their God'.

evidence.source: And my tabernacle shall be in them: & I will be their God, and they shall be my people
evidence.target: I will set my tabernacle in the midst of you

37:27.note: Ezekiel's restoration promise gathers Leviticus 26:11-12 into one verse — the tabernacle set among them, God theirs, they his people. The Apocalypse takes the same promise up at 26:12 (entered separately).

evidence.source: my sabbaths I gave to them, to be a sign between me and them: & that they might know that I am the Lord sanctifying them
evidence.target: it is a sign between me and you in your generations: that you may know that I am the Lord, which sanctify you

20:12.note: Ezechiel re-utters God's Sinai word almost verbatim: the sabbaths given 'to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord sanctifying them'.

evidence.source: which a man doing, shall live in them
evidence.target: which a man doing, shall live in them

20:11.note: Ezekiel, rehearsing the gift of the statutes in the wilderness, quotes Leviticus' own promise attached to them word for word. Paul quotes the same clause at Romans 10:5 (seed-carried).

evidence.source: Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers
evidence.target: so that you shall eat the flesh of your sons & of your daughters

5:10.note: Ezekiel re-pronounces the covenant curse of Leviticus 26 as present judgment on Jerusalem. The siege of Samaria enacts it literally (4 Kings 6:29, entered as parallel).

evidence.source: approached not to a menstruous woman
evidence.target: To a woman, having her flowers, thou shalt not approach

18:6.note: Ezekiel's portrait of the just man is a digest of the holiness code; this clause is Leviticus 18:19 in the prophet's own dress.

evidence.source: hath not lent to usury, and not taken more
evidence.target: Thou shalt not give him thy money to usury, and an overplus of the fruits thou shalt not exact of him

18:8.note: The paired marks of the just man — usury not charged and 'more' not taken — are Leviticus 25:37's own pair: money to usury, overplus exacted. Psalm 14:5 sings the same clause (entered separately).

evidence.source: And I will sanctify my great name, that is polluted among the Gentiles, which you have polluted in the midst of them
evidence.target: Pollute not my holy name that I may be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel

36:23.note: Leviticus ends the priestly charges with the command not to pollute the Name, that it be sanctified in Israel's midst. Ezekiel takes the charge up for the exile, where the Name was polluted among the Gentiles instead. Matthew 6:9's 'hallowed be thy name' reaches Leviticus through this verse and is set aside as mediated.

evidence.source: they shall teach my people what is between a holy thing and polluted, & between clean and unclean they shall shew to them
evidence.target: that you may have knowledge to discern between the holy and profane, between the polluted and clean

44:23.note: The charge given to Aaron after the death of Nadab and Abihu — to discern between holy and profane, polluted and clean — is handed on to Ezekiel's temple priests as their teaching office.

evidence.source: All carrion, and thing taken by a beast of birds, and of cattle the Priests shall not eat
evidence.target: Carrion and that which was taken of a beast, they shall not eat, nor be polluted in them

44:31.note: Leviticus' carrion ban for the priests is re-enacted nearly word for word in Ezekiel's temple law.

evidence.source: widow, and her that is divorced they shall not take for wives, but virgins of the seed of the house of Israel
evidence.target: but a widow and her that is put away, and a filth, and a whore he shall not take, but a maid of his own people

44:22.note: Ezekiel's temple law extends the high priest's marriage rule — no widow, no divorced woman, a virgin of his own people — to all the priests of the restored house, with one stated exception for a priest's widow.

evidence.source: And my sheep were dispersed, because there was no Pastor: & they came to be devoured of all the beasts of the field, and were dispersed
evidence.target: lest the people of our Lord be as sheep without a pastor

34:5.note: Ezechiel's charge against the shepherds of Israel opens where Moses' prayer began: a flock with no pastor is a flock dispersed and devoured.

evidence.source: And this is the border of the land: toward the North quarter, from the great sea by the way of Hethalon, as they come to Sedada
evidence.target: from the which they shall come unto Emath as far as the borders of Sedada

47:15.note: Ezechiel's survey of the restored land retraces this chapter's borders: the north line still runs from the great sea by Emath toward Sedada and Enan (34:7-9) — the old lot lines kept for the new possession.

evidence.source: In that day shall that which is upon the bridle of the horse be holy to our Lord
evidence.target: wherein thou shalt grave after the work of a graver, Holy to the Lord

14:20.note: The words graven on the high priest's golden plate — 'Holy to the Lord' — are in Zacharias' last day found upon a horse's bridle: the inscription itself is quoted and spread over all Jerusalem.

evidence.source: shall go up from year to year, to adore the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the festivity of tabernacles
evidence.target: From the fifteenth day of this seventh month, shall be the festivity of tabernacles seven days to the Lord

14:16.note: The feast given to Israel in Leviticus 23 is opened by Zechariah to 'all that shall be left of all Nations': every surviving people goes up to Jerusalem from year to year to keep it.

evidence.source: Behold thy gods Israel, which brought thee out of the Land of Ægypt
evidence.target: These are thy gods Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Ægypt
